name: policy-based-design
intent: Assemble a class's behaviour, structure and defaults from small interchangeable policy units bound when the host type is instantiated, so that each orthogonal design decision can be varied independently instead of being frozen in the class's code.
problem: A reusable class hard-codes several independent design decisions - allocation, ownership, storage, threading, validation, error handling - inside its implementation, so a different combination is only reachable by editing or copying the class, while the runtime Strategy alternative costs a virtual call per use and gives up the guarantee that the choice is fixed, inlineable and checked before the program runs.
context: Generic library and framework code in languages whose type system can bind behaviour to types - C++ templates and concepts, Rust trait bounds, Scala contextual abstractions, and to a lesser degree C#, Kotlin, Swift and TypeScript generics: several orthogonal axes vary independently, the variant is known when the host type is instantiated, and the component is a widely reused primitive or a hot path where a virtual call, an allocation, or a per-instance configuration flag is undesirable.
benefits: Combinatorial reuse: a handful of policy classes on a few orthogonal axes produce an exponential family of host types from a small core of code (Alexandrescu's SmartPtr: four policies, hundreds of combinations).
Orthogonal decisions become explicit, named and localized: each axis (storage, ownership, checking, threading) has one policy class and one documented contract instead of a buried design choice.
Zero-cost variation where the language monomorphizes: policy calls bind statically, inline, and need no vtable, so an instantiated host is indistinguishable from hand-specialized code.

Client-side extension without touching the library: a user writes a policy class against the documented contract and mixes it with the canned ones, so the component is open-ended rather than a closed family.
In modern toolchains the policy contract is checked at the binding site (C++20 concepts, Rust trait bounds, declared interfaces and protocols) instead of failing deep inside the host body.

Policies can enrich the host with additional members (public base members in the classic form, protocol extensions or conditional impls elsewhere), giving optional functionality with graceful degradation.
tradeoffs: Type explosion: every policy combination is a distinct type, so compile times and binary size grow, and hosts parameterized differently cannot share a container; explicit instantiation and fewer axes are the usual mitigation.

The policy contract is documented, not declared, in the classic duck-typed form: a missing or misspelled member fails only at instantiation (pre-concepts) with a wall of template errors, and a member the host does not exercise can be silently wrong.

No runtime variation: any choice driven by configuration, user input or a plugin must be rebuilt or wrapped in a second, runtime-dispatched layer (Strategy objects, type erasure) that duplicates the abstraction.

Non-orthogonal axes: policies that interact (ownership with conversion, checking with storage) multiply the test matrix and can produce combinations that compile but are semantically wrong, because the compiler checks syntax and not intent.

Debuggability and diagnostics: monomorphized, inlined policy calls disappear from stack traces and debugger frames, breakpoints hit every instantiation, and errors often surface far from the policy that caused them.

Refactoring and ABI cost: changing a policy contract recompiles every instantiation and every policy, and in C++ the host and its policies must stay visible in headers, so the abstraction leaks into build times and binary boundaries.

participants.responsibility: The parameterized type the client instantiates: it owns the primary algorithm and routes each orthogonal decision to the policy bound to that axis.

The named, documented contract - the members a conforming implementation must provide for one behavioural axis - which the host relies on and which is enforced by the toolchain where the language allows it.
One implementation of exactly one policy (RefCounted, SingleThreaded, NoChecking, LruStorage, ...); not intended for standalone use, only composed into a host.
Chooses the policy classes and binds them to the host at instantiation, thereby fixing the design decisions; may also supply a custom policy class for an unforeseen need.
A policy that other policies use as a shared hook - e.g. a threading model, logging sink or allocator - so that cross-cutting defaults propagate to every axis.

use_cases: Library primitives with several orthogonal decisions: smart pointers (ownership, checking, conversion, storage), object pools and allocators (allocation, threading), hash containers (hasher, equality, allocator) - a few policy classes covering an exponential family of types.
Numerical and algorithmic kernels that must run checked (assertions, bounds checks) in debug builds and unchecked in release builds without maintaining two parallel class hierarchies.
Object factories and registries whose creation method is the axis (new, clone/prototype, arena, pooled) while the lookup algorithm stays fixed - Alexandrescu's Creator/PrototypeCreator example.

Reusable components whose logging, locking or serialization strategy must be chosen per product configuration: no-op versus real logger, single-threaded versus thread-safe, compact versus verbose encoding.
Framework and standard-library style extension points: a component that must accept a user-written hash, comparison or allocation policy without being modified and without a class hierarchy.
Compile-time configuration of a data structure's shape (node layout, cache size, index arithmetic) where the decision is a type-level or constant policy rather than a value passed at run time.
Rust's std::collections::HashMap<K, V, S> makes hashing a type-bound policy: S implements BuildHasher and defaults to RandomState, while with_hasher selects a custom builder for specialized maps.
C++'s std::unordered_map<Key, T, Hash, KeyEqual, Allocator> exposes hashing, equality, and allocation as independent template policy parameters with standard defaults.

.NET 7 generic math uses C# static abstract interface members (for example INumber<TSelf>) so generic algorithms bind arithmetic behavior through a constrained type parameter instead of a runtime strategy.
avoid_when: The behavioural variant is selected at run time - from configuration, user input or a plugin registry: use Strategy objects or functional interfaces injected through the constructor (dependency injection), or a type-erasure wrapper; policies are fixed when the host type is instantiated.

The class is not a reused primitive: for a single type that will never be instantiated with another policy set, a plain implementation - or a protected virtual step in a Template Method - is simpler and keeps call sites and error messages readable.

The language cannot bind behaviour to types or erases type parameters (Java, Go in practice, C without macro machinery): express the variation as a Strategy interface or an interface-typed field instead of emulating templates.

The axes interact heavily or the contract cannot be stated as a small set of operations: the host becomes an untestable matrix of combinations whose invalid pairings still compile; split the component or make the interaction an explicit policy.

Compile time, binary size or ABI stability dominates - a widely included header or a library with a stable binary interface: per-combination instantiation and header-visible policy bodies are the wrong trade there.
anti_patterns: Policies that carry no behaviour - type aliases, constants or empty marker types - so the host is just a parameterized data structure and callers gain no leverage from the extra parameters.
Calling unrelated free functions from the host while calling it policy-based composition: there is no documented contract and no named axis, so a contract change breaks every host silently.
Passing an already-built runtime object into a template host and calling it through a virtual interface: the design pays the template complexity and the dispatch cost at the same time.
Reflexive decomposition into dozens of single-member policies ('policy soup') with no orthogonal structure, making instantiation sites unreadable and error messages unusable.

Using a policy-parameterized host as a configuration mechanism with exactly one instantiation per product: a family of types exists on paper while nothing varies, hiding a plain class behind template noise.
design_principles: Separation of concerns and single responsibility per axis: each policy owns exactly one design decision, and the host owns only their composition.
Open/closed: new behaviour enters through new policy classes, not through edits to the host.
Composition over inheritance: policies are combined to build a host rather than organized as a subtyping hierarchy; where inheritance is used it is implementation reuse, not an is-a relationship.
Dependency inversion at the type level: the host depends on the documented policy contract, never on concrete policy implementations.
Interface segregation: the policy contract is the narrowest set of members the host actually exercises, kept explicit so policies stay interchangeable.
best_practices: Enumerate the design decisions first, give every axis a policy with a two-part name (Storage, Ownership, Checking, ThreadingModel), and merge axes that always change together.

Write the policy contract down - members, semantics, pre/postconditions - and enforce it where the language allows (C++20 concepts or static_assert, Rust trait bounds, C#/Swift/Kotlin interface or protocol constraints) so a wrong policy fails at the binding site.

Give every policy parameter a sane default, keep policy classes small, stateless and non-polymorphic (in the classic C++ form: protected non-virtual destructor, no virtuals), so clients bind only the axes they vary.
Never use policies for runtime variation: expose a Strategy or type-erasure wrapper at the host's boundary when the decision must be made after instantiation.
Keep instantiations under control: explicit instantiation or extern templates, one alias per product configuration, and no policy parameter that only one call site ever binds.
Test the host against a deliberately odd policy, not just the canned ones, and add a compile-time contract check (concept/static_assert/trait bound) for every member the host relies on.
sources: Andrei Alexandrescu, Modern C++ Design: Generic Programming and Design Patterns Applied (Addison-Wesley, 2001) - Chapter 1, Policy-Based Class Design.
